As of 830 PM EDT Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Showers continue overnight, but the threat for
any strong storms has ended. 

Latest WX analysis indicated the sfc front situated near of just
S of the NC border. There was a distinct DCAPE gradient and 
despite very weak shear, some storms were able to become briefly
strong along with localized heavy rainfall. In general, the
threat for any additional strong storms has now ended w/ the
loss of daytime heating and the latest SPC mesoanalysis now
showing CIN across the region. Showers are developing across
portions of central VA to the north of the front, and will 
become more widespread overnight over the NW 1/2 of the CWA, but
additional tstms are unlikely or will be isolated. Lows tonight
will range from the mid be in the mid 60s NW to the lower 70s 
SE. 

On Tuesday, the Canadian high pressure shifts a bit eastward, 
serving as a reinforcement of our onshore flow. Northeast winds will 
begin to pick up along the Eastern Shore Tuesday morning, then 
spreading to all coastal locations through the day. Widespread 
(coastal) gusts to 25mph will be likely, with gusts increasing to 35 
to up to 45 mph along the Atlantic coast of the Eastern Shore 
(including Ocean City, Chincoteague, etc) Tuesday night into 
Wednesday. The lingering front will keep rain chances going on 
Tuesday for most of the area. Could get some isolated storms as well 
that create locally heavy downpours and instances of flash flooding. 
WPC has highlighted the western half of the area in a Day 2 Slight 
ERO. Highs will range from the upper 60 N-NW to the low-mid 80s 
across southern portions of the area. The cooler airmass will make 
its presence known starting Tuesday night as lows will be in the mid 
50s across the northwest, with low to mid 60s inland and upper 60s 
along the SE and coastal areas. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Persistent onshore flow and a strengthening coastal 
low will create a wetter, cooler, and breezier forecast for most of 
the week.

Cold air damming will overtake the area on Wednesday as high 
pressure remains parked to our north. This will keep high 
temperatures in the low to mid 60s for the northern and western 
inland areas, with low to mid 70s for the SE half of the CWA. Winds 
for coastal areas will persistently be blowing around 20-25 mph with 
gusts to 35+ mph. The strongest winds will once again be along the 
Atlantic coast of the Eastern Shore with gusts to 40-45 mph likely 
Tuesday night, potentially lasting all the way through at least 
Thursday as the low pressure remains offshore. Rain chances continue 
everywhere on Wednesday, though due to the stable cooler 
environment, storms aren't expected, with the exception of the NC 
coast. There could once again be areas of locally higher rainfall at 
times that lead to flash flooding. WPC has a Marginal Risk of 
Excessive Rainfall for a majority of the area on Wednesday. Rain 
chances may focus more across the eastern portions of the area later 
Thursday into Friday. A secondary surface low may form and cause the 
main low to recenter itself slightly closer to the Mid-Atlantic/New 
England coast late Thursday into Friday. Highs will remain in the 
60s with 70s closer to the coast both day. If winds are able to 
shift more out of the north around the west side of the low 
pressure, our low temperatures Thursday and Friday night could dip 
into the mid 50s, with the potential for even some upper 40s well 
inland. 

Into the weekend and beyond, models are showing that this low may 
continue to hang around to our northeast. As of right now, it still 
appears that it will be just far enough from our area that we may 
have a pleasant weekend for most of the area, but that definitely 
could change as the details of the low's placement come to light. Be 
sure to stay tuned to the latest forecast updates as this system 
will create a prolonged period of gusty onshore winds, coastal 
flooding, high surf, beach erosion, and dangerous marine conditions 
(see below). 


KEY MESSAGE 3...Coastal Flood Watches have been issued for a large 
majority of the tidal area starting Wednesday afternoon/evening high 
tide as widespread moderate to locally major tidal flooding 
(inundation of 2-3 feet AGL in vulnerable areas) is likely to strong 
northeast winds. Tidal flooding is expected to continue for several 
tide cycles (potentially through the end of the work week) given the 
persistent northeast winds.

Strong northeast winds are expected from Tuesday night through at 
least Thursday, which will cause water levels to rise across much of 
the area (especially along the bay, tidal rivers, and Atlantic 
coast). No worse than nuisance-minor tidal flooding is expected 
through Tuesday evening. Tidal anomalies will then significantly 
rise on Wednesday due to strong persistent NE winds. Minor flooding
